en: Take my blood, poured into a leather flask!
My wolf-maned lion, listen well:
If you would take my head, here I am!”
As he spoke and pleaded,
The lion did not heed him.
“A shrew remains in Talas,” he said;
The wolf-maned one gave it no thought.
“Does one whose death has come not die?
When a living person remains,
Does he not go on saying, ‘I will not die’?
When the Creator in truth
Gives his true command,
When Gabriel, the taker of souls,
Comes to take a life,
Laying all five fingers upon it,
When he comes to take the soul,
The tongue is bound and cannot speak.
If it truly comes, death’s arrow,
What person can escape?
When death truly comes,
Does the poor mortal not die?
Will the dug grave not take him in?
Will the black earth not contain him?
‘A wretched wife, a young child
Were left behind in Talas’—
Do not rave like that, Shuutu!
In Beijing that Solomon never touched,
While I stand ruling here,
Without opening their eyes wide,
Without curbing their wicked ways,
Without restraining their wilfulness—
Without gathering gold and coins,
From this Beijing where I stand,
How can I leave without shame?
If this is a land Chalyar never touched,
This Great Beijing lying here,
If I raised dust among its people,
Poured out its people's blood,
And was the one who conquered it,
‘Wife and child in Talas’—
What aim would that fulfill?
Since I mounted the golden throne,
Not even six full months have passed;
How can I go back to Talas?
Without ruling Beijing three years,
How could I return to Talas
And bear to stay there?
Let what I gathered scatter if it must;
My Prophet is true, my faith is true;
Faith is what I pray for!
This very year, warrior Shuutu,
I shall grasp my spear and break their ranks;
If death comes, I shall fall to a bullet!”
Saying thus, your ocean,
“All the seven khans,
The twelve Muslim khans,
Leaving none of their soldiers behind,
Let them all bring them and come.
Without delay, all of them,
Let them all be ready!” he said,
And sent warrior Ürbü galloping.
In Beijing where Solomon never came,
The Muslims who had taken rule
Had become men of sacred power.
The twelve khans, each apart,
Had become khans in twelve places.
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan,
In the city of the Black Kalmyks,
Have you heard the news?
Over Khan Zholoy's people,
Old Koshoy was khan.
Khan Zholoy, khan of the Kalmyks,
And Khan Koshoy of the Katagan,
Having fought each other since long ago,
Had an ancient feud.
When Aykhozho's Bilerik
Had fallen captive,
Fighting against Zholoy,
Suffering real hardship,
Shooting at each other twelve years,
The khan skilled among spearmen,
All the warriors had gathered.
Fighting for so many years,
Brave men had been slaughtered.
For this reason Khan Koshoy
Was taking his ancient revenge,
Inflicting so much grievous torment
Upon the Kalmyks.
Laying taxes on the Kalmyks,
Making them yellow as with jaundice,
Taking tribute, driving them to distress,
Having the people's gelded goats gathered,
Having their goats slaughtered,
Having cattle hair chopped fine,
And sprinkled into their mud,
About six thousand of their champions,
Putting hoes into their hands,
He made cut and tread the clay.
From the many Kalmyks there,
He had fired bricks made and brought.
“Let the fame of what I have done
Last until the Day of Judgment,” he said,
And had a mosque founded and built.
All the prominent people
He made gird their waists tight.
Those who said, “I shall become Muslim,”
In the milk of white-grey mares
He had bathed and washed.
Those pure white, clear of dirt,
To the young men who had come unmarried
He insisted on marrying them.
It had become an example;
Such was the tale of the warriors.
Those who had survived the dead,
From the Kalmyks and Chinese,
That was where they got offspring:
Fermented mare's milk by day, girls by night,
That was the people living in pleasure.
The Chinese were a prolific people;
It was a land flooded with light.
Though slaughter lasted forty years,
Not seeing it as slaughter at all,
They were a people who never looked back.
What Khan Koshoy had done,
Let us leave it there.
The youngest of nine sons,
A servant of the one God,
Who dwelt in Maseyil,
Called the mightiest warrior of them all,
Eleman's warrior Töshtük,
In the ridge of Alachang,
In the mines where gold was dug,
With gold and gold coins
Had had his fill just then.
When he went beneath the earth,
Had his reason been burned away?
All of the Torguts
He ruled, boiling up their misery.
“For three households to milk,” he said,
And had a single goat tied up.
The Torgut people wailed:
“Beijing that the Holy One never touched
Has now lost all its means!”
They all sobbed and cried out.
Who ruled the people, making them cry,
Let us leave warrior Töshtük.
Khan Buudayyk's Muzburchak,
Let us begin to speak of him.
Khan Buudayyk's Muzburchak
Had been an unbroken wall.
See the command of Him who writes fate:
In Börüköz's place,
He had mounted the throne as khan.
In the city where the Sibe lived,
He had become a khan of sacred power.
He had the face of the earth opened,
Had its sand spread far and wide,
Had grain widely sown,
Had abundance flourish,
Had their mules, donkeys and horses
All tethered in their places.
Bending as they danced,
Many Sibe bowed:
“When Börüköz was here,
Owning no land even a kidney's size,
We were poor and wretched.
With Muzburchak here,
All of us have prospered alike!”
Thus the Sibe sang,
Playing their flutes.
“When Börüköz was here,
We withered,” they said.
“How could we not have withered?
Whenever it suited him,
He would turn the water elsewhere.
About seven thousand yearlings still nursing,
Pacers no wind could catch, abundant wealth,
Every year, beating us,
He took them from us as tribute.
When Muzburchak came to us,
Our hearts became peaceful;
What we ate became butter!”
Saying thus, the Sibe
Stood rejoicing;
Every day they held a spring feast.
A khan from among the Muslims:
It was the time they had taken Beijing.
His yurt walls were made of wood,
His first forefather was Alash;
Warrior Kökchö, Aydarkan's son,
Had become a man of sacred power,
Had become khan over the Solon.
Those who met his wrath,
He made bend their knees to the earth;
Those who offended him,
He made run up and down.
He had their valuables taken as plunder;
With himself at the head of the Kazakh army,
He had destruction brought upon their people.
Their white-bearded old men
He made work raw hides;
Those who had grown decrepit
He made dance for amusement.
All the Solon gathered,
Unable to endure it, perishing.
Warrior Kökchö kept them hemmed in.
All of the Solon
Warrior Kökchö kept beating.
Ruling the people by beating them:
Such was warrior Kökchö's khanate.
In little Kökchö,
There was that rashness.
Was he not, by his fathers' ways,
A Kazakh from of old,
Who husked his millet clean as stones,
Who praised his wife as a maiden,
Who dwelt in Sary-Arka,
The Kazakh people, sons of their fathers?
If not for generous Manas,
The multitude of Kazakhs in Sary-Arka
Had never seen Beijing before.
When dear Manas in Beijing
Waged a mighty war,
The Muslims had been his support.
Their twelve armies, so many people,
On every side among the Chinese,
Were exercising rule;
The Muslims were reigning as khans.
When warrior Ürbü on his black horse
Before Khan Manas
Had driven every one of them,
The great army gathered.
Within that army
Were their khans Koshoy and Töshtük,
Azhybay and Bakay were there too,
Their tigers Almambet and Syrgak,
The forty companions, champions and wolves.
There were old men among the elders;
Aykhozho who had come from Mecca
Was also there to lead the faith.
With words he had to say,
The son of Khan Kökötöy,
Their lord, warrior Bokmurun, was there.
There were khans of the common people;
Warrior Shygay from the Oyrat,
That warrior was there as well.
The elders' courts, the blue-clad retinues,
Great Kokand and Margalan,
Had come to fight.
Kozubek, khan of Kokand,
Malabek of Margalan,
Fork-bearded Synchybek of Andijan,
That warrior was there as well.
They had come from India too.
